summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension that lets an IKEv2 security association be created and authenticated without creating a Child SA. It is experimental and an independent submission, not an Internet Standards Track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally two computers that set up an encrypted connection also agree there and then how to protect the traffic. Sometimes there is no traffic to protect yet, or the peer only wants to be checked that it is who it claims to be. RFC 6023 lets the two sides authenticate each other and set up their secure channel without agreeing anything about traffic protection.

questions: create ikev2 sa without child sa
how to create an ikev2 sa without a child sa
why use ikev2 only for authentication
subtitle: An IKEv2 extension that sets up and authenticates a security association without also creating a Child SA.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 requires the authentication exchange to try to create a Child SA as well as the IKEv2 SA, which is inconvenient when a peer only wants to be authenticated or has no traffic to protect yet.
tldr.mechanism: The responder advertises a CHILDLESS_IKEV2_SUPPORTED notification in its IKE_SA_INIT response. If that notification is there, the initiator may send a modified IKE_AUTH request with the SA payload and the traffic selectors left out.
tldr.outcome: The two peers end up with an authenticated IKEv2 SA and no Child SA. This is an Experimental independent submission, not a standard.

today: RFC 6023 is an Experimental independent submission that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification: the RFC Editor published it for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and says it makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment. It extends the base IKEv2 specification in RFC 5996.

sections.title: Why an IKEv2 SA Without a Child SA
sections.content:
IKEv2, as specified in RFC 5996, requires that the IKE_AUTH exchange try to create a Child SA along with the IKEv2 SA. The memo says this requirement is sometimes inconvenient and sometimes superfluous. Some implementations need IKEv2 for authentication only, and others would like to set up the IKEv2 SA before there is any actual traffic to protect. The extension described here allows the creation of an IKEv2 SA without also attempting to create a Child SA.

An IKEv2 SA with no Child SA is not a fruitless endeavour. Even without Child SAs, an IKEv2 SA allows the checking of the peer's liveness status through liveness checks, the quick setting up of Child SAs later without public key operations and without user interaction, the authentication of the peer, and the detection of NAT boxes between two hosts on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up the secure channel is separate from deciding how to protect the traffic that will travel through it. This memo lets the two sides do the first part on its own, when there is nothing yet to protect.

sections.title: Where It Helps
sections.content:
The memo lists several situations that led to the proposal. In an interactive remote access VPN, the user tells the client to connect, which may involve interactive authentication, and there is still no traffic. Because there is no traffic, it is impossible for the gateway to know what selectors to use, which are the rules for narrowing down the client's proposal. With location-aware security, a user roaming between trusted and untrusted networks should have all traffic encrypted on the untrusted network, while on the trusted network only the IKEv2 SA needs to be maintained. An IKEv2 SA may be needed between peers even when there is no IPsec traffic at all, because such peers use liveness checks and report the status of the VPN links to an administrator.

Other cases include IKEv2 on physically secure links, where authentication is necessary but traffic protection is not, such as the Passive Optical Network links described in a 3GPP report. The memo also points to EAP-IKEv2 in RFC 5106, where IKEv2 is used as a method of user authentication, and to the case of a node that receives IPsec traffic with an unrecognised SPI and should send an INVALID_SPI notification, which it can do in a protected INFORMATIONAL exchange if it first sets up an IKEv2 SA. Finally, a future extension may use IKEv2 SAs to generate keying material for applications, in the way RFC 5705 does for TLS.

In some of these cases it might be possible to create a dummy Child SA and then remove it, but the memo says that creates undesirable side effects and race conditions, and that the IKEv2 peer might see the deletion of the Child SA as a reason to delete the IKEv2 SA as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Several situations need a secure channel with nothing flowing through it yet: a remote worker who has connected but not sent anything, a device moving from a trusted network to an untrusted one, a link that is physically secure already, or a node that only needs to send one warning message.

sections.title: How Support Is Agreed
sections.content:
The decision whether to support an IKE_AUTH exchange without the piggy-backed Child SA negotiation is ultimately the responder's. A responder that supports the extension must include the notification described in the next section in its IKE_SA_INIT response. A supporting initiator may then send the modified IKE_AUTH request, and it must not send that modified request if the notification was not present.

A responder that has advertised support must process a modified IKE_AUTH request and must reply with a modified IKE_AUTH response. It must not reply with a modified IKE_AUTH response if the initiator did not send a modified IKE_AUTH request, so that an ordinary exchange is never answered with something unexpected.

A responder that has been configured not to support the extension must behave as if it did not support it. It must not advertise the capability with a notification, and it should reply with an INVALID_SYNTAX Notify payload if a client sends an IKE_AUTH request modified in the way the memo describes. That gives a client that tries the extension against an unwilling peer a clear error instead of silence.
sections.plainLanguage: The side that answers decides whether the shortcut is on offer, and says so in its first reply. The side that asks may only use the shortcut when that offer was made. A peer that does not support it says so clearly, so a mistake shows up as an error rather than as a hang.

sections.title: The Notification and the Modified Exchange
sections.content:
The notification is an ordinary IKEv2 Notify payload. Its protocol ID, one octet, must be 1 because the message relates to an IKEv2 SA. Its SPI Size, one octet, must be zero, in conformance with section 3.10 of RFC 5996. The notify message type, two octets, must be 16418, the value assigned for CHILDLESS_IKEV2_SUPPORTED.

The modified IKE_AUTH exchange is shown for the Extensible Authentication Protocol version of an AUTH exchange, since the non-EAP version is very similar. What is missing from the request and the response is set out in the memo: the optional notifications IPCOMP_SUPPORTED, USE_TRANSPORT_MODE, ESP_TFC_PADDING_NOT_SUPPORTED and NON_FIRST_FRAGMENTS_ALSO; the SA payload; the traffic selector payloads; and any notification, extension payload or VendorID that has to do with Child SA negotiation. The EAP exchange itself is otherwise unchanged, with the same sequence of requests and responses as the base protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer is a small extra field in the first reply, carrying the number 16418. The modified exchange is the usual one with the parts that talk about protecting traffic removed, so both sides authenticate each other and stop there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This protocol variation inherits all the security properties of regular IKEv2 as described in RFC 5996.

The memo adds one point of its own. The new notification carried in the initial exchange advertises the capability, and cannot be forged or added by an adversary without being detected, because the response to the initial exchange is authenticated with the AUTH payload of the IKE_AUTH exchange. It also notes that both peers have to be configured to use this variation of the exchange in order for the responder to accept a childless proposal from the initiator, so the extension is off unless it is deliberately turned on at both ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed by the shortcut, and the offer itself cannot be faked because it is covered by the authentication that follows. Both sides have to switch the feature on for it to be used at all.
